.@fal's Gorkem Yurtseven and Batuhan Taskaya on making an open source video model 35x faster, and what Hollywood wanted after they built it:

Last month, MiniMax released H3, an open source video model. fal rebuilt it - they cut down the steps the model takes to make a video, rewrote the code under each stage, and got the GPUs to 70-80% of their theoretical ceiling instead of their usual 30-40%. No quality loss.

Video now generates faster than you can film it. The models have gotten so cheap and fast that end users aren't even asking for improvements in either category anymore. The gap has moved to quality, or how closely the model follows the prompt.

Hollywood wasn't a customer a year ago and is now fal's fastest growing segment. Studios love it for the little things - extending a shot, moving the camera, changing the lighting. Those edits land 80-90% of the time. fal is chasing 99.9%.

It’s interesting that many people  take it as a given that unlike virtually any technology in the past, whoever is first to develop “AGI” will gain some kind of permanent monopoly and chokehold on economic and political power. This would be unlike any technological development in history.

- the US had a monopoly on nuclear for four whole years 
- the USSR’s satellite lead lasted just four months 
- Europe built airplanes within years of kitty hawk / planes were diffused by WWI
- Bell had a 20 year patent monopoly on telephones that didn’t last 
- the transistor diffused instantly 
- the creator of the internet DARPA captured no rents 

The bomb is the closest analogy to a decisive strategic advantage but even then, scientists who felt they had an allegiance to transnational Marxism or to keeping the balance of power intact exfiltrated the technology almost immediately. The breakthrough also signaled to other programs that success was possible, dramatically changing odds of success. 

The bomb also demonstrates that the US institutionally LACKS the decisive ability to execute some kind of a pivotal act eg by forcibly suppressing all rival models that are close to AGI. We weren’t able to do it with nukes when we were an uncontested superpower, we certainly won’t do it today. 

The available evidence also suggests that weights diffuse relatively quickly - the open weight models are only a few months off the frontier and are rubber banded forward via distillation as the labs keep pushing. If you can fit an entire model on a flash drive I have a hard time believing it will remain the exclusive purview of one organization. 

The people who believe that AI is a winner takes all technology in which the first to RSI gains a permanent monopoly owe it to us to explain how exactly this would work. Why can’t two labs reach RSI? Arguably, this is the case today. How would the leading lab suppress its competitors? Prevent distillation or exfiltration? 

If your safety thesis rests on the premise that the first to RSI/AGI/ASI will be uncontested, you owe us an explanation of how this would work and why historical precedent should be thrown out.

All this fear around AI taking your job misses a huge part of the story...

Labour force participation was falling long before AI showed up because it follows the birth rate with a twenty year lag, and birth rates have been falling for decades. 

So machines are mostly filling the gap left by people retiring or leaving the workforce anyway. That's a very different picture from the one you're being sold.

The old GDP equation ran on population growth plus productivity growth... synthetic labour removes that ceiling entirely. Productivity keeps compounding without needing more people to do it. 

That's the Economic Singularity, and it changes the whole equation.

This is the biggest problem in American politics.

For 50 years, corporate profits averaged roughly 7% of national income. Today, corporate profits account for more than 14%.

In today’s dollars, that difference is about $2 trillion per year.

There is no single explanation for why this shift occurred, and it certainly isn’t just one thing.

This isn’t all bad either. A larger corporate profit share helps explain why corporate earnings and asset prices have risen so strongly relative to the economy and to history, benefiting many people.

But the distributional effects of this shift are substantial, and they help explain why so many people feel the current system isn’t working for them.

This trend has been developing for nearly 30 years and spans political parties.
